`category` is protected from a caller-supplied metadata delta by a TWO-LAYER split, not by one rule: the service layer carries it through a `replace` structurally (option (a) of the review's two suggested fixes), while the MCP boundary rejects only the explicit attempts to destroy it (`metadata_delete_keys=['category']`, and a `metadata_patch` category value outside the `MemoryCategory` enum). The review's option (b) — rejecting any `metadata_mode='replace'` whose `metadata_patch` omits `category` — is deliberately NOT taken.</decision>
<parameter name="rationale">The two options differ in who bears the burden and what the failure mode is when they get it wrong. Option (b) makes every replace caller restate `category` on every call: a routine tag edit (`metadata_patch={'topic': 'cgl-eta'}, metadata_mode='replace'`) becomes an error, and the caller's fix is to copy a value it must first read back — a read-modify-write it would otherwise never need, and one it can get WRONG, silently re-categorizing the record. That turns a loss-prevention rule into a new source of the same loss. Option (a) has no such edge: the key survives by construction, and `new_custom.update(metadata_patch or {})` already lets an explicit `metadata_patch={'category': ...}` override the carried value, so deliberate re-categorization keeps working with no special case. It also mirrors the shape already shipping one line away — mem0-owned keys are re-attached automatically rather than demanded from the caller — so a reader meets one protection idiom, not two. The boundary rules then cover what option (a) structurally cannot: a delta that NAMES the key. Splitting them by layer is what makes each honest. The service layer's job is preventing SILENT loss, and it must hold for every caller including the in-process recon Stage 1 dispatch, so it lives in `_apply_metadata_delta` where both write routes already converge (INV-5 — patching the `overwrite_payload` route and the `mem0.update` fold separately would let the semantics drift, which is exactly why step 20 consolidated them). The boundary's job is refusing a self-reported external caller's explicitly destructive intent, which is a policy question about untrusted input and belongs where the other reserved-key rejections already are — not duplicated into the service, where it would be a second copy free to drift. Recorded because a later reader finding a rule at only one of the two layers will otherwise read the asymmetry as an oversight and 'fix' it by duplicating.</rationale>

<parameter name="decision">Declare `stamped_at` as an OPTIONAL `str | None = None` field rather than making it conditionally required for `kind='found_on_main'` in `_check_conditional_requirements`.</parameter>

More importantly, ABSENCE is deliberately load-bearing: because every write after this lands populates the field at the chokepoint, a blob lacking it provably predates task 3576. That is exactly the signal the soak-gate predicate uses to separate legacy backlog from new stamps, so the field must be allowed to be absent.</parameter>

<invoke name="mcp__plan-tools__add_design_decision">
<parameter name="decision">Populate `stamped_at` for `kind='found_on_main'` only, not for `merged` or the `deterministic-*`/`operational-verified` kinds.</parameter>
<parameter name="rationale">Matches the task's stated scope, and keeps blast radius minimal: the resolved-provenance dict is asserted on by a large existing suite, and a non-deterministic value appearing on every kind would perturb `merged`-kind assertions across the interceptor and boundary tests for no benefit. `merged` already has strong independent landing evidence (merge-queue journal + is_ancestor + commit citation, task 2500); `found_on_main` is precisely the attribution-by-inference kind that lacks it. A later task can widen the field if another kind needs the same signal.</parameter>
</invoke>
<invoke name="mcp__plan-tools__add_design_decision">
<parameter name="decision">Legacy (unstamped) flagged tasks are still returned and still PRINTED by the predicate, but are excluded from the exit-code gate via a separate `gating_offenders()` filter.</parameter>
<parameter name="rationale">Silently dropping them would make the gate structurally blind to any future write path that bypasses `_validate_done_provenance` — an unstamped-but-new blob would be classed legacy and never gate. Reporting them with an explicit `stamp_class=legacy` marker honours the project's loud-over-silent-degradation norm and the design invariants' no-silent-fail-soft rule: the operator still sees all 13 known offenders in the log, they simply stop forcing EXIT 1 on a soak gate whose question is "has anything NEW gone wrong since --since". Keeping the split in a separate pure helper (rather than filtering inside `find_spurious_since`) also leaves the existing `find_spurious_since` tests green.</parameter>
</invoke>
<invoke name="mcp__plan-tools__add_design_decision">
<parameter name="decision">The A/B sub-pattern split (legitimate named-sibling attribution vs. spurious bare-merge-commit sharing) is computed from COMMIT FAN-OUT over the audit report, not from the new timestamp.</parameter>
<parameter name="rationale">This refines the task description's stated root cause. A stamp-write timestamp cannot distinguish the two sub-patterns — they differ in citation shape, not in time; two tasks stamped the same second can be one legitimate and one spurious. Fan-out (count of distinct found_on_main task ids per cited commit) measures exactly that, and is derivable from data the predicate already holds. So the two signals are kept orthogonal and both delivered: `stamped_at` supplies freshness scoping (which is what genuinely required a new field, and what actually stops the EXIT-1 loop), fan-out supplies the sub-pattern classification.
